entries.name: Smart Augmentation
entries.definition: A learned augmentation procedure that trains a network to synthesize examples from same-class inputs while receiving both a within-class reference loss and feedback through the target classifier’s training loss.
entries.identity_notes: Smart Augmentation denotes Lemley et al.’s learned same-class synthesis procedure, not all automatically chosen augmentation policies. It differs from fixed averaging in SamplePairing, convex input/target interpolation in MixUp, adaptive coefficient regions in AdaMixUp, and adversarial or latent-data generative formulations. The two networks cooperate through training losses; a generator does not by itself imply a GAN minimax game. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 253 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 27 lines in each checkout. These were neighboring-record and review references or prior candidate leads, not existing records for these identities. Twelve exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: Same-class input selection and a reference loss encourage class-consistent outputs but do not certify semantic label preservation or membership in the true data manifold.
The paper’s optimality and convergence language describes the intended training behavior; no proof of globally optimal augmentations or universal generalization improvement is asserted.
The reconstruction and classification terms can compete, and their weighting and schedule affect the learned generator. A synthetic output need not look like a natural image to be used by the method.

The concrete channel-stacking, MSE and categorical-cross-entropy setup is one published realization. The record does not make the experimental architecture, alpha/beta values or number of augmenters universal requirements.

claims.statement: During training, an augmentation network A takes same-class examples and produces a synthetic example of the original sample type and spatial shape. A reference example from that class supplies an augmentation loss L_A, while a target network B supplies its task loss L_B. Backpropagate through B into A using a combined objective f(L_A,L_B), which may be weighted or scheduled. A can be shared across classes or specialized into separate class-dependent networks. In the published grayscale realization, stack k same-class input images as channels, produce a one-channel image, and choose an additional same-class reference that is not one of those inputs. L_A is mean squared error to this reference; B processes the generated image and the reference as separate examples with categorical cross-entropy L_B. Figure 9 combines losses as alpha*L_A+beta*L_B. At test time discard A and use B on ordinary examples. Multi-example blending is the central construction, while the reported experiments also include a one-input setting; fixed channel counts, architectures and weights are protocol choices.

entries.name: SamplePairing
entries.definition: An image-classification augmentation procedure that averages an anchor image with a randomly selected training image using equal pixel weights and trains against the anchor image’s label, with a training schedule that includes phases without pairing.
entries.identity_notes: SamplePairing is the equal-image-weight, anchor-label procedure of Inoue, distinct as a training protocol from the standard Beta-distributed input/target MixUp construction. This distinction does not imply that every expected objective differs: under exchangeable pairing and a loss linear in targets, averaging the anchor-label losses over both orders matches the half-and-half target loss for the same averaged image. The paper itself discusses this relationship. It is also distinct from learned Smart Augmentation and from spatial patch replacement in CutMix. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 253 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 27 lines in each checkout. These were neighboring-record and review references or prior candidate leads, not existing records for these identities. Twelve exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: Averaged images can contain incompatible classes; the assigned anchor label is a training convention, not a claim that the mixture has a unique correct semantic label.

The paper’s N-squared count describes ordered pairing choices. Commutativity and duplicate inputs can make different pairings produce the same averaged image, so it is not a guarantee of N-squared distinct visual samples.

The expected-loss relation to half-and-half soft labels requires the stated symmetry and loss assumptions. It does not equate individual sampled gradients, arbitrary pair distributions, the full training schedules or the original randomly weighted MixUp procedure.

The source’s training-accuracy ceiling discussion is idealized and does not establish a universal bound for every finite training run. No benchmark advantage, training-cost equivalence or medical-task result is imported.

claims.statement: For a training anchor, randomly select a partner from the training set without requiring the same class. Apply ordinary image augmentations to the inputs when used, then average corresponding pixels and channels with equal weights. Train on the mixed image using only the anchor label; the partner label is not required by this rule. The published training schedule starts without SamplePairing, enables it after a warm-up, intermittently disables it during training, and finishes with a no-pairing fine-tuning phase. These numerical intervals are experimental choices, not the identity of every use. A learned augmenter, a random mixing ratio, same-class pairing and label interpolation are not required by the original procedure.

entries.name: CutMix
entries.definition: A training augmentation procedure that replaces a rectangular region of one image with the corresponding region of another and mixes their class targets in proportion to the retained and pasted image areas.
entries.identity_notes: CutMix is spatial patch mixing with area-weighted targets. It is distinct from whole-image intensity averaging, zero masking, learned synthesis and hidden-representation interpolation. The record describes input-image CutMix; feature-level variants are not silently treated as an identical architecture or layer. Its official implementation profile is pinned separately from the proceedings formula. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 253 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 27 lines in each checkout. These were neighboring-record and review references or prior candidate leads, not existing records for these identities. Twelve exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: Patch area is a heuristic for class-target contribution; it need not equal the visible object area or semantic information retained. A pasted patch may contain background or remove the discriminative object region.

Integer side lengths, floor division and boundary clipping make the actual area differ from the nominal Beta draw. The realized target coefficient is not generally distributed as the original Beta variable.

The pinned training code uses one application decision, rectangle and coefficient for a minibatch and a random permutation for partners. Per-example variants and feature-level CutMix require separate version-specific descriptions.

The script’s beta argument controls the Beta distribution, while alpha controls PyramidNet width; these names are not the paper’s mathematical alpha convention. Default beta and cutmix_prob are zero, so the augmentation must be enabled by configuration.

The implementation was read, not executed. Old API usage and unspecified runtime dependencies preclude an execution guarantee. Logged training error against the anchor labels is distinct from the mixed-target training objective. No universal localization, robustness or performance improvement is asserted.

claims.statement: Choose two training images and a binary spatial mask M. Construct M*x_A+(1−M)*x_B, preserving anchor pixels outside the rectangle and using donor pixels inside it. Train against lambda*y_A+(1−lambda)*y_B, with lambda representing the retained anchor area fraction. The paper draws a nominal coefficient from Beta(alpha,alpha), samples the rectangle center uniformly over the image, and sets nominal side lengths to the image dimensions times sqrt(1−lambda). The published experiments use alpha=1. The donor patch is taken from the same spatial coordinates as the overwritten anchor region. Unlike MixUp, individual pixels are selected from one source rather than blended throughout the image; unlike Cutout, the removed region is filled with another training image and target weights reflect both sources. On a discrete image, clipping and integer box construction can change the nominal area, so the inspected implementation recomputes the target coefficient from the actual rectangle.

claims.statement: When beta is positive and the minibatch application draw passes cutmix_prob, the pinned implementation samples a Beta coefficient, permutes the batch, constructs a shared rectangle and replaces that region with the permuted donor pixels. rand_bbox converts each nominal side length to an integer, uses half-width floor division on each side of a random integer center and clips endpoints to the image dimensions. It then sets lambda=1−rectangle_area/image_area and sums lambda times the anchor cross-entropy with 1−lambda times the donor cross-entropy. With this shared coefficient, the objective equals cross-entropy against the correspondingly mixed targets. Training continues by backpropagation; ordinary unmodified inputs and labels are used when the application condition fails.

native_neighbors.name: MixUp
native_neighbors.definition: A training-data interpolation procedure that fits a predictor to convex combinations of example inputs and their corresponding targets using the same random mixing coefficient for both.

claims.statement: Draw pairs (x_i,y_i) and (x_j,y_j) from the training data and lambda from Beta(a,a), a>0. Construct x_tilde=lambda*x_i+(1−lambda)*x_j and y_tilde=lambda*y_i+(1−lambda)*y_j, then minimize the prediction loss on these mixed input-target pairs as an empirical vicinal risk. The classification example mixes one-hot labels into soft targets; the formulation is expressed for feature-target vectors. The source presents paired minibatches and also describes mixing a minibatch with its random shuffle. Its Figure1 uses one sampled coefficient for a paired minibatch; this is not a requirement that every variant share one coefficient. As a tends toward zero from above, the interpolation distribution concentrates at the endpoints, recovering empirical-risk training in that limit. The original rule does not replace lambda by max(lambda,1−lambda); that first-example-majority convention belongs to the later MixMatch family.

evidence.locator: Section 2 and Figure 1, PDF/printed pp. 2–4; core vicinal distribution and interpolation rule on p. 3

aio_mappings.rationale: The procedure constructs virtual training pairs by interpolating existing examples. The AIO target is data augmentation in a preprocessing branch, whereas this local record also specifies target interpolation and predictor training; this is a related association, not equivalence or a subclass claim.
The original method trains against interpolated observed targets. The target is the supervised learning task; this is an algorithm-to-task association.

limitations: Inputs and targets need meaningful convex combinations in compatible vector spaces. Interpolations need not be natural samples or remain on a data manifold.
Linearity between examples is an inductive bias, not a guarantee that the ground-truth conditional labels interpolate linearly or that accuracy and robustness improve.
Beta(a,a) requires a>0; the empirical-risk limit a→0 is not a valid Beta(0,0) sampling instruction.
No performance result, particular network architecture, fixed alpha or sampling implementation is asserted.

native_neighbors.name: Manifold Mixup
native_neighbors.definition: A neural-network training procedure that interpolates paired examples’ representations at a selected network layer and interpolates their labels with the same coefficient, then trains the entire network on the mixed representation-target pairs.

claims.statement: Select a layer k from an eligible set S, which may include the input layer. Forward a minibatch and its randomly shuffled copy to layer k. Draw lambda from Beta(a,a), a>0, and mix both the paired layer representations and the paired one-hot targets using lambda and 1−lambda. Continue the forward pass from the mixed representation and compute the prediction loss against the mixed soft target. Backpropagate through the whole graph, including the network before the mixing layer, so the representations themselves can adapt. The reported implementation choice uses one layer and one coefficient per minibatch. With only the input layer eligible, S={0}, the objective reduces to original input MixUp; allowing hidden layers is the distinguishing extension. The objective averages over examples, mixing coefficients and eligible layers.

evidence.locator: Section 2 and Equation (1), PDF p. 3; theoretical scope in Sections 3.1–3.2, PDF pp. 4–5

native_neighbors.name: AdaMixUp
native_neighbors.definition: An adaptive interpolation-training procedure that learns example-dependent mixing-coefficient regions with a policy network and trains a classifier together with an intrusion discriminator intended to separate mixed examples from original data.

claims.statement: For a pair of examples, a policy-region network outputs a three-component softmax (alpha,delta,remainder). Interpret the first two components as the interval(alpha,alpha+delta) for the mixing coefficient. Sample epsilon uniformly on(0,1) and set gamma=alpha+delta*epsilon so gradients can pass through the interval parameters. Form gamma*x1+(1−gamma)*x2 and the correspondingly mixed class targets. Train the classifier with observed and mixed targets, and train the policy generator together with an intrusion discriminator to distinguish generated mixtures from original examples. The discriminator shares the classifier’s feature network while using its own final classification layers. For higher-fold mixing, reuse the same pairwise generator recursively by mixing an original example with an original or previously mixed example; composing a previous coefficient vector lambda with coefficient gamma gives (gamma*lambda,1−gamma). The paper describes alternating minibatch optimization of classification/mixup loss and intrusion loss. Its intended intrusion supervision treats mixed examples as outside and observed examples as inside the data manifold; this is a learned surrogate, not direct access to the true manifold.

native_neighbors.name: Bayesian Data Augmentation for Deep Models

claims.statement: Treat each additional labeled example z=(t_a,x_a) as a latent variable and seek a maximum-a-posteriori parameter estimate, rather than sampling a posterior over all network weights. The generalized M-step seeks parameters that increase this sampled objective rather than solving a global maximization exactly. The published objective includes a parameter prior, an average of real-data label/data log terms and a separate average of synthetic-data label/data log terms. In the paper’s concrete GAN realization, a class-conditioned generator produces labeled images, a classifier learns dataset labels on real and generated examples, and a separate authenticator distinguishes real from generated images. J_C separately averages the real and synthetic classification losses, rather than averaging one pooled batch with weights determined solely by its real-to-synthetic count ratio. The GAN architecture is one realization of the augmentation framework, not a requirement for every possible realization.
